desc: This station involves assessing and resuscitating a woman who deteriorates in day-surgery recovery after a dilatation and curettage, escalating for suspected uterine perforation, and then explaining the PALM-COEIN classification and why obesity raises endometrial cancer risk.
explain:
Fat in the curettings

Fat in the curettings means the curette or other instrument has passed through the uterine wall into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat. It is a red flag for uterine perforation, even when the procedure seemed uneventful. The risk is higher in obese women and in those with a retroverted or fixed uterus. The dangers are haemorrhage from uterine or pelvic vessels, and unrecognised bowel or bladder injury, which can lead to peritonitis. This patient's tachycardia, hypotension, drowsiness, worsening pain, peritonism and shoulder-tip pain suggest bleeding or peritoneal irritation.

Management is simultaneous resuscitation and escalation. Use an ABCDE approach, titrated oxygen, two large-bore cannulas, crystalloid and early bloods including group and crossmatch. Activate a MET call if deterioration criteria are met, and call the senior gynaecologist urgently. Give analgesia, keep her nil by mouth and start IV antibiotics per eTG. Unstable or peritonitic patients need urgent laparoscopy or laparotomy to look for visceral injury. Stable patients may have urgent CT as directed by the senior. Document, practise open disclosure and file an incident report.

PALM-COEIN (FIGO 2018)

PALM-COEIN classifies the causes of abnormal uterine bleeding. The structural causes are Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma and Malignancy and hyperplasia. The non-structural causes are Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorder, Iatrogenic and Not otherwise classified. This patient has irregular cycles and heavy bleeding with obesity and diabetes, so ovulatory dysfunction is the most likely category. However, a 14 mm endometrium at 51 years, with her risk factors, means malignancy and hyperplasia must be excluded by histology. Several categories can coexist.

Why obesity raises uterine cancer risk

  • Adipose tissue aromatises androgens to oestrone, raising circulating oestrogen.

  • The oestrogen is unopposed by progesterone. Progesterone is absent after menopause, and low in obesity-related anovulation before menopause. Unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation, hyperplasia and endometrioid cancer.

  • Hyperinsulinaemia and raised IGF-1 further promote endometrial proliferation.

Family history

Ask about endometrial, bowel and ovarian cancer in relatives. A single first-degree relative with bowel cancer at 54 does not meet the usual Amsterdam II or revised Bethesda thresholds for Lynch syndrome, which generally involve younger onset or multiple affected relatives. A fuller family history is still warranted.
guide:
A high-performing candidate starts resuscitation straight away with an ABCDE approach, large-bore access, fluids, a crossmatch and a MET call, while taking a brief history. They recognise that fat in the curettings means uterine perforation, call the senior gynaecologist urgently and consider bowel or other visceral injury. They explain honestly to the patient, including that results are pending. They then list all nine PALM-COEIN categories, identify ovulatory dysfunction in obesity while keeping malignancy and hyperplasia in mind, and give all three obesity mechanisms.

A borderline candidate takes a long history before resuscitating, or treats the pain as routine postoperative pain and gives analgesia alone. They may not link fat in the curettings to perforation, or may forget to escalate urgently. They recall only part of PALM-COEIN and explain obesity only as 'more oestrogen' without the absence of progesterone or the insulin and IGF-1 effect.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Jenny Okafor

  • Age: 51-years-old

  • Gender: Female

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No

  • Location: Day-surgery recovery bay, 3 hours after hysteroscopy and D&C under general anaesthetic

Presenting complaint: Worsening lower abdominal pain since waking from the anaesthetic

History (give only if asked):

  • Pain began about an hour after you woke and was mild at first. It is now 8/10, constant, across the lower tummy, and worse with movement or deep breaths.

  • Pain in the tip of the right shoulder.

  • Feels dizzy, sweaty, nauseated and very sleepy. You answer questions slowly but correctly.

  • Vaginal bleeding: a small amount on the pad, much less than your usual periods. No clots.

  • You have not vomited and have not passed urine since the operation.

  • You do not know what the doctor found during the procedure.

  • Allergies: nil known. Medications: metformin only. No blood thinners. Last ate eight hours before surgery.

  • Last cervical screening test was normal.

Examiner to provide when the candidate performs each step:

  • Airway: patent, speaking in short sentences

  • Breathing: RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air, chest clear

  • Circulation: HR 118, BP 92/58 (was 125/75 pre-operatively), cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds

  • Disability: GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6), drowsy but rousable, BGL 9.8 mmol/L

  • Exposure: temperature 36.9 °C, small amount of blood on the pad

  • Abdomen: lower abdominal tenderness with guarding and rebound, reduced bowel sounds

Actor cues:

  • Appear pale, sleepy and distressed by pain. Wince on abdominal palpation.

  • Ideas: you think the pain is just from the operation, but it feels much worse than expected.

  • Concerns: ask quietly, "Did they find cancer? Is something wrong with me?" Be reassured by honesty and a clear plan. Accept that results are not yet back.

  • Expectations: you want the pain to stop and want to know what is happening.

Examiner prompts:

  • Task 2: if not mentioned, ask "What does the fat in the curettings suggest, and who do you need to involve?"

  • Task 3: if the candidate has not addressed it, ask "Which PALM-COEIN category fits this woman best, and why does her weight matter for cancer risk?" If time allows, ask "Is there anything in the family history you would explore further?"

  • A one-example-per-letter list is not required. Marks are for what each letter stands for.

The candidate should interact with you using non-medical terminology. Please interrupt if medical terminology that would not be understood by the lay public is used.
points: Fat in curettings after D&C means uterine perforation until proven otherwise: resuscitate, call the senior gynaecologist urgently and assess for bowel or other visceral injury.
In a deteriorating post-procedure patient, use ABCDE with simultaneous resuscitation, group and crossmatch, and activate a MET call when criteria are met.
PALM-COEIN: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia, Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorder, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified.
Obesity raises uterine cancer risk through aromatisation of androgens to oestrone, unopposed oestrogen (anovulation or menopause) and hyperinsulinaemia with raised IGF-1.
A single first-degree relative with bowel cancer at 54 does not meet Lynch criteria alone, but a fuller family history of endometrial, bowel and ovarian cancer is warranted.

stem:
You are the gynaecology resident on call at a metropolitan public hospital. You have been called to the day-surgery recovery bay to review Jenny Okafor, a 51-year-old woman who had a hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage (D&C) three hours ago for eight months of heavy, irregular vaginal bleeding.

Pre-operative summary (from the chart):

  • BMI 41 kg/m2, type 2 diabetes on metformin, nulliparous

  • Cycles irregular for two years, with heavy bleeding for eight months; not on anticoagulants or hormones

  • Pre-operative transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 14 mm, no discrete polyp or fibroid seen

  • Cervical screening test up to date and normal

  • Mother diagnosed with bowel cancer at 54 years

The recovery nurse tells you she is worried about the patient. She also mentions that the scrub nurse noted yellow, fat-like tissue in the curettings container. The operating registrar has since gone to another theatre.
tasks: Assess the patient: take a brief focussed history, perform an ABCDE assessment with initial resuscitation and examine the abdomen. Explain to the patient what you are concerned about and what will happen next (3 minutes).
State to the examiner your working diagnosis with the significance of the fat in the curettings, and outline your further management and escalation (2 minutes).

Explain to the examiner what each letter of PALM-COEIN stands for, which category most likely explains this patient's original bleeding, and why obesity increases her risk of uterine cancer (3 minutes).
title: Severe abdominal pain after curettage for abnormal bleeding
